en: *Śikṣāsamuccaya-kārikā-śāstra*, one fascicle.
Composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by imperial decree.
If one sees the physical form of a woman, Or her radiant and seductive grace,
The fool fails to understand and Falsely gives rise to lustful defilement.
The Buddha taught [meditations on] the bloated corpse and so forth To eliminate thoughts of sexual desire.
One who can follow the teachings of the World-Honored One attains the supreme fruit and nothing else.
With pure precepts, learning, and reflection, exerting oneself in constant cultivation,
and binding mindfulness to contemplate all objects— this is the cause of liberation.
If a person has the defilement of anger, as well as dullness and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt— these five obstruct the cultivation of concentration.
Having little learning, living among the crowd, and delighting in base matters— these three obstruct the cultivation of wisdom.
Attachment to the body and its enjoyments, And likewise, they can obstruct the concentrated mind.
There are five conditions for mental distraction: The mind scatters following various objects;
Relishing [meditative states], as well as sinking and agitation, Pride, and a heavy craving for fame.
A bhikṣu relying on the noble teaching should confess and eliminate any transgressions;
skillfully taking up the objects of mental focus is the primary practice.
Next, one should rely on a place of tranquility where all hindrances and difficulties are absent.
Thereafter, one should cease perverse thoughts; this is the primary task of a bhikṣu.
One should dwell in a cemetery, wear robes of discarded rags, constantly seek the state of tranquil rest, and sever the mind of lustful defilement.
When a mendicant sees a woman, he should contemplate her as impure;
with eyes restrained and wrong thoughts eliminated, he should take his food with a focused mind.
He must distance himself from excessive speech and worldly affairs.
When afflictions arise and press upon you, you must endure them through the power of wisdom.
Whether beneath a tree, amidst a heap of grass, or dwelling within a mountain cave, one should remain in such places when observing the times; in such tranquility, the mind may be cultivated.
When practicing concentration and taking an object as one's focus, one should not be too high or too low;
one should not be too close or too far, but rather bring oneself into correspondence with the object.
One should properly grasp the focal object and examine it with meticulous care.
When closing the eyes and dwelling in the mind, it is as if seeing with eyes open.
All sense-gates are withdrawn and gathered; abiding in mindfulness, one concentrates the inner mind.
Contemplating the object appearing before one, one causes this state to continue from moment to moment.
Regarding the previously grasped signs, one contemplates their form and appearance with focused attention:
the swollen female organ is terrifying, loathsome, and base.
It is like the water of a turbid pool, stirred and shaken by the wind.
When observing the shadows of the trees, they do not remain clearly distinct;
when the water of the mind’s defilements and afflictions is stirred by the wind of distracted emotions,
even when one observes with a settled mind, the darkness cannot remain.
When the mind sinks, one should uplift it with exertion; One may contemplate sublime and wondrous objects.
Just as a leech, exhausted from drinking blood, Is revived by being sprinkled with water;
So too, one should quickly withdraw and collect the mind, And settle it securely within its former object.
One should make the mind pliant, so that it is well-tamed and follows every thought.
If the mind becomes agitated, one should contemplate things that inspire weariness;
thus the mind is made to abide in tranquility, like a hook pulling back the head of an elephant.
Distant from both dullness and agitation, one should direct the mind with equanimity;
abiding in equanimity according to the natural state, at this time there is no fault.
From this point, gradually attaining stability, the mind rests peacefully upon the reflected image of the sign.
Clearly understanding the practice of the Middle Way, hold the lamp of right mindfulness to illuminate.
At this time, employ investigation and analysis; one should observe in successive order until the image of meditative concentration arises and remains clearly manifest before one.
Unwavering and luminously pure, like the form of a great man— this reflection,
when compared with the former, is the mark of distinction.
Once this mark has arisen, desire, craving, and the like are immediately eliminated.
This is the person who binds the mind; it is the preliminary sign of the first dhyāna.
Next, one knows that the essence of anger originally arises from the defilement of craving;
once sensual desire has been eliminated, one attains freedom from anger.
Next, by applying diligent mindfulness, one dispels the mind of drowsiness and lethargy;
once the specific characteristics have been observed, doubt is immediately stilled.
Next, one should eliminate remorse and proceed upon the secure path of virtuous conduct.
Tranquil and unobstructed, it is able to prevent restlessness.
One should know that by employing coarse vitarka, one contemplates the perceived characteristics;
then, within the reflection of the mind, one investigates with subtle vicāra.
Seeing these distinctions, the mind rejoices; from this, one attains pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
Next, one realizes the meditative absorption of bliss (*sukha-samādhi*). Such are the successive factors of concentration (*samādhi-aṅga*), which constitute the fundamental dhyāna (*mauladhyāna*).
One then establishes the mind of mindfulness (*smṛti*) with perfect stability.
Just as one who wishes to reach a village, and having reached the village itself,
once the fundamental concentration (mauladhyāna) has been attained, performs further cultivation to acquire the knowledge of others' minds,
the recollection of past lives, the supernormal powers, and the divine eyes and ears.
When there is still applied thought (*vitarka*) here, the mind is unable to abide in tranquility;
it is like a river with waves—know that this is not the case for the higher stages.
Having attained the first dhyāna, one continues to abide upon the object of focus.
Next, relying on the second dhyāna, vitarka and vicāra are both stilled.
Although one abides in this state, one is still drifted by the waters of joy;
upon entering the third dhyāna, the mind then dwells in tranquility.
Because his mind possessed pleasure, he was unable to abide in mindfulness;
once he had realized the four dhyānas, all faults were eliminated.
There are the stages of decline, of progress, of stability, and of penetration.
There are four kinds of dhyāna, which the practitioner of concentration should first know.
If a concentration accords with the afflictions, it is called the "part conducive to decline";
that which is superior to the latter is the "part conducive to excellence," and one should know that which abides in itself as the "part conducive to maintenance."
Because they arise from prior skillful discernment, they are the cause for the path of penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*).
Since this concentration can bring that about, it is called the "part conducive to penetration.
Regarding the characteristics of impermanence and so forth, one forms the realization of them as suffering and so on.
If one attains this meditative concentration, it constitutes the stages of the path such as "heat" (*uṣmagata*).
Regarding the signs of blueness, bloatedness, and so forth, there are many ways of observing the object;
one should understand the distinctions according to the practice taught in the Noble Teachings.
The corpse’s belly is distended by the wind, with pus flowing from its orifices;
the joints and thighs are all swollen and coarse—this is called "bloated.
One does not find the coarse parts of the body desirable, yet craves only the fine and smooth skin.
For those whose minds are stained by passion, one should cause them to cultivate this contemplation:
when a portion of a corpse has a slight flow of whitish pus and the remaining flesh is mostly bluish, this is called the "blue-swollen" stage.
Seeing a form and giving rise to desire is what is called "one who loves forms";
its antidote is the bloated blue corpse, as taught by the Sun-like Kinsman (the Buddha).
When pus flows everywhere from a corpse, this is called the "sign of flowing pus."
To those who are attached to the fragrance of a person, he causes them to contemplate the cessation of defiled desire.
When a corpse’s waist has rotted and severed, it is called the "sign of disintegration.
To those who are attached to a whole body, the Great Sage spoke [of this].
The corpse is devoured by foxes and raccoon-dogs; As birds peck at it, only residual sinews remain.
To counteract attachment to the skin and flesh, I describe for you the appearance of the remains after eating.
The various bones of the limbs, hands, and feet Are scattered in every direction.
For those whose minds are dominated by craving, one teaches the visualization of the disordered skeleton;
then, regarding that very disordered skeleton, one causes them to visualize it being severed and torn apart by knives and clubs,
even while they still desire the body as a whole, thereby causing them to contemplate the sign of its violent destruction.
The corpse is hacked by knives, or wounded by spears and arrows;
blood flows over its mangled body, which is termed the "blood-smeared" aspect.
Its body is anointed with pure fragrances, newly adorned with colorful garments.
For those who give rise to desire toward this, it serves as an excellent medicine.
Since they cherish only this object and do not permit others to look upon it,
one should observe how many worms devour the corpse, thereby causing them to eliminate their evil thoughts.
When flesh and bones have all dissolved away, only the teeth and bone remain;
for those who give rise to craving for the teeth, cause them to contemplate the characteristics of the teeth and bone.
If one sees a recently deceased person, whose consciousness has departed yet whose physical form remains, [one should likewise contemplate it].
Sentient beings delight in and cling to greed; may they be made to eliminate their coquettish desires.
Excrement, urine, mucus, and saliva—these thirty-two kinds of substances gather together to form the body; this leather bag is what is called a "person."
Hair, fur, nails, and teeth; liver, stomach, and other organs—these depend on one another.
Within, three hundred bones provide support, while nine hundred tendons crisscross in binding.
From nine apertures flow impurities; their filth and stench are beyond description.
Carefully examining what is truly loathsome, the wise should not associate with it.
Having observed the bodies of other women, one should likewise scrutinize one's own form;
regarding this cause of lustful defilement, one ought to maintain constant mindfulness.
One does not escape the prison of the triple world; it all stems from a mind stained by desire.
Therefore, the wise person reflects most carefully upon this matter.
Having endured the sufferings of many hells, one has fortunately attained a human body.
How could one allow the wild mind to run rampant, failing to cultivate sublime practices?
There are many varieties of lustful craving, arising with differing attachments;
a single contemplation can eliminate them all—this is called the Contemplation of White Bones.
Forms, touches, shapes, and seductive gestures, And the silk tassels that breed defiled attachment— What medicine can remove these? None surpasses the contemplation of white bones.
First, at the big toe of the foot, Fix the mind and visualize it as a festering sore.
Once destroyed, pus flows forth, and the flesh all falls away.
One then contemplates the shape of the finger bone, which is like the color of a white dove;
as the ulcer gradually expands, the skin and flesh are entirely removed.
Proceeding in this sequence, one removes all flesh from the body until it is entirely gone;
through the perfection of right mindfulness and resolute understanding, one contemplates only the skeleton.
If even a fragment of flesh remains, it is called a distracted mind.
How much more so when the monkey of the mind is let loose, racing toward and seeking various objects.
Having first mastered the ability to remain well-settled through prolonged concentration on one's own thoughts,
one then gradually extends this to others, contemplating them all as skeletons.
Gradually expanding until reaching the edge of the ocean, the space is filled entirely with white bones;
once this concentration has been accomplished, one abandons the vastness and makes it narrow again.
When contracting, one begins by abandoning from the outside, until only the bones of one's own body remain.
Returning the observation to the tips of the toes is the sequence for this concentrated mind.
At times, one may gradually relinquish the body part by part until reaching the skull bone;
one should know that the final moment of mind should be gathered and stabilized between the eyebrows.
If one practices this cultivation, one will always be born in the sublime Brahma palaces and not fall into the three miserable realms, but attain birth in the five pure abodes.
The wholesome deeds performed with a distracted mind in the human world merely cause one to flow back into the river of birth and death.
The wise person cultivates a concentrated mind, As if extinguishing fire upon one's body or clothing.
One may then abandon all external conditions And dwell in the quietude of the forest.
Do not allow impermanence to press upon you, So that you die in vain with a distracted mind.
With a mind purified by *prajñā*, one will ultimately obtain desirable fruits;
as one does not wish for further existence (*punarbhava*), so should one cultivate the supreme path.
Having shaved one's hair and donned the *kāṣāya*, one ought to cultivate the Noble Path.
All other clamorous and distracting matters are causes for birth and death.
The Seventy Verses on the Practice of Calm Abiding and Insight.
